title: Pay scale, the union and Right to Work
summary: Gigs follow union scale, but the union lost power after Right to Work laws; society values music less.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: What’s the average — I don’t know if you can say what an average gig is — what’s the pay scale like in New Orleans? Is it possible to say?

Yeah. I think that the pay generally speaking, and you know, how should I put this, we have a musician’s union in New Orleans. And I could speak for myself. Most of the gigs that I play are in line with what the pay scale is of the union. Yeah. About what the union pays. This is a big, it’s always a big discussion with musicians now, that there was once a time when most of the gigs in New Orleans were union gigs, and the union was very strict about making sure that the union musicians who were performing on those gigs, and they were getting union scale, those days are gone. But what I’ve heard, and I haven’t really done any research about this to really know exactly what the cause of this was, but there was some type of laws that changed, called the Right to Work laws, and I think maybe it was in the late 80’s, something like that. And I mean just generally speaking to other musicians, this is kind of the feedback that I get, and some of them say okay, this is what changed everything for us, and this is when the union no longer had the power that they had.
Yes, I did hear something about that.

So now, so what that meant was then that those club owners were able to start paying musicians, a lot of musicians would either not be union then, of course those musicians would work for less then, so the musicians that were — so that’s difficult. That’s a difficult thing and that’s an ongoing, that’s always an ongoing battle between trying to, if you feel that you’re trying to be at a certain level at your craft and be professional, and then someone who’s hiring you, or hiring that person, will just say well I’ll just get this other person to play for half of what you’re playing. It doesn’t really matter how — I think it’s a lot — if they sound not as good as you, or the band is not as good as you, or whatever. But I think that it’s a lot of different things that contribute to that, I don’t think it’s just one thing, you know what I mean? they did at a time when maybe musicians were making more, as it relates to the cost of living.
